title: KV cache — memory layout, fragmentation & eviction notes
content:
Purpose
---
Notes and early spec for the KV cache memory layout, fragmentation mitigation, memory pools, and eviction policies for the serving runtime. Goal is a pragmatic design that: keeps tail-latency low, minimizes memory amplification on GPU-hosted KV (pinned host memory / device memory), and gives predictable OOM behavior for multi-tenant workloads.

Scope
- In-memory KV used for model KV caches (Transformer KV caches), prefix caches, and small feature caches inside runtime.
- Target platforms: dedicated GPU servers (host+device), and managed-hosted nodes where we control allocator.
- Exclude persistent disk-backed caches (S3/LevelDB) — those are separate.

High-level requirements (from infra + product)
- Keep per-request latency jitter minimal (no long pauses for GC/compaction).
- Support high churn for interactive workloads (many short-lived keys).
- Support very large keys (up to 32MB, though 95p < 512KB).
- Efficient on-device storage when models pinned to device memory (tight budgets).
- Multi-tenant fairness: per-model quotas and graceful eviction cross-model.

Design constraints and tradeoffs considered
- Slab allocators reduce fragmentation for many small fixed-size KV entries but waste for heterogeneous sizes.
- A single global allocator is simplest; per-model pools improve isolation but can increase fragmentation if not right-sized.
- Compaction (moving live objects) reduces fragmentation but is expensive and adds pauses — we prefer incremental background compaction where possible.

Proposed architecture overview
- Top-level: KVCacheManager orchestrates pools, eviction, and cross-pool policies.
- Pool types (hierarchy):
  1) Tiny-slab pool: for entries <= 256B. Packed slabs with bitmap freelists. Low overhead, high density.
  2) Small-slab pool: for 256B < size <= 8KB. Multi-slot slabs (power-of-two bucket sizes: 512, 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K).
  3) Large-pool (segregated): for sizes > 8KB. Uses large-region allocator with an LRU-style free list and best-fit-ish search.
  4) Huge-chunk allocator: for entries > 512KB. Allocated with page-aligned mmap/alloc to avoid copying — tracked separately for eviction.
- Metadata store: dense side-table per key that stores key_id, size_bucket, pool_id, LRU-timestamp (or epoch), pin_count, tenant/model tag. Stored in a compact hash table (open addressing) optimized for lookups during generation.

Memory layout details
- All slab pools allocate large superblocks (2MB or 8MB depending on pool) from the OS (or host pinned allocator). Superblocks are subdivided into slots.
- Superblock header includes generation id + free bitmap; header is colocated at superblock start to keep scan quick.
- Align slots to 16B to improve SIMD-friendly copies and reduce unaligned writes to GPU DMAs.
- Large-pool regions are chunked into power-of-two ranges and tracked with a segregated free-list; we keep per-size-class freelists to avoid scanning.

Fragmentation mitigation strategies
1) Size bucketing + slab reuse: for the majority of small KV entries, slabs minimize internal fragmentation. Choose bucket sizes by p95/p99 analysis (see experiments below).
2) Per-model soft quotas: prevents a noisy tenant from consuming all small slots; when a model crosses quota, mark low-priority entries for accelerated eviction.
3) Background compaction for large-pool: compact live chunks into new contiguous allocations when fragmentation exceeds threshold (e.g., >25% external wasted space). Compaction is incremental and rate-limited; we avoid moving pinned device memory unless model is pinned to device and we have a device-to-device copy path.
4) Deferred free + epoch reclamation: frees are recorded into batch queues and reclamation happens at safe points to avoid ABA issues with concurrent schedulers.
5) Coarse-grained defragmentation windows: schedule compaction during low-util windows (based on traffic monitor).

Eviction policy options (tradeoffs)
- Baseline: segmented LRU with size-awareness (LRU that accounts for cost = size * recency_weight). Simpler and predictable.
- Cost-aware probabilistic eviction: compute eviction score = alpha * size + beta * (now - last_used) + gamma * model_priority. Choose thresholds to favor dropping large cold entries first.
- Tenant-aware fairness: global eviction loop selects victims from per-tenant candidate lists proportionally to overusage.
- Pin/unpin semantics for active in-flight requests. Pinned entries are excluded from eviction.
- Fast-path cold eviction: maintain tiny bloom filters and compact LRU lists per bucket so evicting small slots is O(1) without global scans.

Preferred hybrid (practical) policy
- Keep per-pool LRU lists (one per slab class + per-large-pool). On eviction event, pick victim pool by "pressure score" (pool_free / pool_capacity). Within chosen pool, evict from tail. Apply size-aware kick: for large-pool use cost-aware selection.
- When global pressure across pools high, perform cross-pool rebalancing: optionally steal a few slabs from low-pressure pools to satisfy urgent allocations. Make this stealing bounded (N slabs per second) to avoid oscillation.

Allocator and scheduling interactions
- Synchronous allocation should be fast-path: try per-thread cache for small slabs to avoid locking. Fallback to atomic bitmap ops on superblocks.
- On allocation failure, trigger async eviction background worker to free up space; but if request is latency-sensitive (marked), fallback to serving with degraded model variant instead of blocking. This ties into smart routing and graceful degradation.
- Eviction work runs at low-priority thread pool. For hard OOM risk (near-critical), escalate to synchronous eviction up to a bounded amount before failing allocation.

Device (GPU) specific notes
- Prefer keeping KV cache for active models in pinned host memory and only move to device when model pinned to device. Device allocations are expensive and we treat device pools as fast but tiny (hard cap).
- Use device-friendly alignment (256B) and keep metadata on host. If moving KV to device memory, maintain host shadow pointers for metadata and a compact relocation table.
- Limit device compaction to times when model pinned exclusively to node. No cross-model device compaction unless both owners agree (rare).

Telemetry and observability
- Emit metrics per-pool: capacity_bytes, used_bytes, free_chunks, fragmentation_ratio (external/internal), evictions/sec, avg_eviction_size, avg_alloc_latency.
- Per-tenant metrics: tenant_used_bytes, tenant_evictions, tenant_blocked_allocs.
- Traces for allocation path (histograms) and compaction batches (how many moved, time per MB).

Experiments to run (short-term)
1) Microbench: synthetic workload with heavy small-churn keys vs heavy large-key workload. Measure fragmentation and eviction frequency over 24h.
2) Heap simulation: feed real production key-size distribution (sample anonymized) to simulator to test slab sizing choices and large-pool thresholds.
3) Device stress: pin a model to device and measure compaction/movement costs with different alignment strategies.

Open questions / decisions needed
- Bucket boundaries: initial suggestion (256B, 512B, 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K). Need to validate against sampled production key distribution (ticket: KV-347).
- Large-pool compaction aggressiveness: threshold and reclaim rate.
- Cross-tenant slab stealing policy: safety bounds and fairness drift control.
- How to surface tenant soft-quota violations to RBAC/CS (alerting UX).

Action items / next steps
- Omar: produce histogram of key sizes from sampled traces (Linear KV-347).
- Priya: implement slab superblock layout prototype and benchmark allocation latency.
- Felix: prototype background compaction worker with rate-limiting knobs.
- Maya (me): draft API for KVCacheManager (pin/unpin, reserve_quota, evict_async) and add metrics names + tags.

Notes-to-self
- Keep eviction deterministic for tests — seed timers/epochs.
- Avoid moving pinned GPU pages unless we can do non-blocking device copies.

References
- internal PR: serving-runtime/pull/812 (prototype allocator)
- Linear ticket: KV-347 (key-size distribution)
- Confluence: Cache-Perf-Playbook (design patterns)

End of doc.
